narrative:
The model determined that you have an 85.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants students likely to succeed, this prediction led to your application being rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily against your application were your class ranking in the third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year class ranking. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure rather than success.

Your third-year ranking placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average ranking of accepted students. This was the single biggest reason the model doubted your chances on the bar. Your LSAT score of 22 was also well below the 37-point average of admitted students, giving the model further reason to expect difficulty passing the exam. Finally, your first-year ranking in the lowest decile, compared with an average around the sixth decile for accepted applicants, added more weight in the same negative direction.

None of these academic signals suggested you were on track to pass the bar. The model therefore concluded the risk was too high.

What you should do next is focus on improving the areas you can control. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, seek academic support to raise your class rankings if you are still in school, and consider strengthening other parts of your record before reapplying. Many students improve these metrics and gain admission on a later attempt.
